evidence.quote:
There were no prisons, no slums, no insane asylums, no cripples, no
poverty, no wars.
evidence.paraphrase: The society has eliminated prisons, poverty, disease, and war.

evidence.quote: All diseases were conquered. So was old age.
evidence.paraphrase: Disease and aging have been cured.

evidence.quote:
The population of the United States was stabilized at forty-million
souls.
evidence.paraphrase: The national population is held fixed at forty million.

evidence.quote: Death, barring accidents, was an adventure for volunteers.
evidence.paraphrase: With aging cured, death now happens only by accident or voluntary choice.

evidence.quote:
Wehling was fifty-six, a mere stripling in a population whose average
age was one hundred and twenty-nine.
evidence.paraphrase: The population's average age is 129, making a 56-year-old young.

evidence.quote:
The room was being redecorated. It was being redecorated as a memorial
to a man who had volunteered to die.
evidence.paraphrase: A room is redecorated to memorialize someone who chose to die.

evidence.quote:
"To be or not to be" was the telephone number of the municipal gas
chambers of the Federal Bureau of Termination.
evidence.paraphrase: A government bureau operates gas chambers reachable by a telephone number.

evidence.quote:
The law said that no newborn child could survive unless the parents of
the child could find someone who would volunteer to die. Triplets, if
they were all to live, called for three volunteers.
evidence.paraphrase: Law requires a volunteer death for each newborn allowed to live.

evidence.quote:
Would you like to go back to the good old days, when the population of
the Earth was twenty billion--about to become forty billion, then eighty
billion, then one hundred and sixty billion?
evidence.paraphrase: Hitz explains the exponential population growth that prompted control.

evidence.quote:
In the year 2000," said Dr. Hitz, "before scientists stepped in and
laid down the law, there wasn't even enough drinking water to go around,
and nothing to eat but sea-weed
evidence.paraphrase: Hitz describes a resource crisis that scientists resolved with population law.

evidence.quote:
"You think this is my idea of what life really looks
like?"
evidence.paraphrase: The painter contrasts the idealized mural with his view of real life.

evidence.quote: "I want those kids," said Wehling quietly. "I want all three of them."
evidence.paraphrase: Wehling expresses his desire to keep all three children.

evidence.quote:
Wehling shot Dr. Hitz dead. "There's room for one--a great big one," he
said.
evidence.paraphrase: Wehling murders Dr. Hitz to make room for a child.

evidence.quote: And then he shot himself, making room for all three of his children.
evidence.paraphrase: Wehling kills himself after two murders to free space for his children.

evidence.quote:
He knew that he would never paint again. He let his paintbrush fall to
the dropcloths below.
evidence.paraphrase: The painter resolves to stop painting and abandons his work after the killings.

evidence.quote:
The painter pondered the mournful puzzle of life demanding to be born
and, once born, demanding to be fruitful ... to multiply and to live as
long as possible--to do all that on a very small planet that would have
to last forever.
evidence.paraphrase: The painter reflects on the dilemma of unbounded life on a finite planet.

evidence.quote: He took Wehling's pistol, really intending to shoot himself.
evidence.paraphrase: The painter picks up the gun intending suicide.

evidence.quote:
a title
no one ever used in conversation. "I should have said, 'Ethical Suicide
Studios,'"
evidence.paraphrase: The official euphemism for the gas chambers is 'Ethical Suicide Studios.'

evidence.quote:
"Your city thanks you; your country
thanks you; your planet thanks you. But the deepest thanks of all is
from future generations."
evidence.paraphrase: The hostess thanks the volunteer on behalf of society and future generations.
